4 Magnetically responsive anisotropy

To validate the key steps in the design of the magnetically responsive anisotropy module, we carried out expression, purification, and fluorescence-based binding experiments for a magnetic-nanoparticle-binding protein. We first obtained a recombinant fusion protein containing the Fe3O4-binding peptide TVNFKLY and completed its expression, purification, and desalting. We then examined its binding to magnetic nanoparticles through FITC fluorescence labeling, co-incubation with the particles, magnetic separation, and washing, thereby providing an experimental basis for subsequently introducing magnetic-field-induced orientation into a SELP hydrogel.

4.1 Design of the Magnetic-Nanoparticle-Binding Protein

Design of the magnetic-nanoparticle-binding protein

Experiment

The Fe3O4-binding capability of

TVNFKLY has previously been validated through phage-display screening and multiple characterization methods [1].

We used TVNFKLY as the functional peptide in the experimental group and included GTWSLLL, which was expected not to bind magnetic nanoparticles, as a control to evaluate the contribution of the TVNFKLY sequence to particle binding. The experimental construct

contained a His tag, a SUMO tag, a

DogTag sequence, and the TVNFKLY

peptide. The His tag was used for subsequent affinity purification, the

SUMO tag helped improve soluble expression and stability of the heterologous protein [2], and DogTag provided an interface for subsequent connection to other protein modules

[3,4].

Because this plasmid differs from the corresponding SUMO-DogTag plasmid by only 81 bp, we used a site-directed mutagenesis system for construction.

The SUMO-DogTag plasmid was used as the backbone, and the TVNFKLY-coding sequence was introduced by high- fidelity PCR. The methylated parental

template was then digested with DpnI, and Exnase II-mediated homologous recombination was used to recircularize the linear amplification product. The recombinant product was transformed into Trelief 5alpha competent cells, and single colonies were picked after selection on kanamycin-containing medium.

Candidate clones were screened by colony PCR, and positive clones were further subjected to plasmid extraction and Sanger sequencing.

Results

We constructed an expression plasmid encoding 6xHis-SUMO-DogTag-TVNFKLY

(Figure 4.1.1).

Single colonies suitable for subsequent screening were obtained on the transformation plates. In the colony

PCR assay, multiple candidate clones exhibited the target band indicated in the original experimental records.

Agarose gel electrophoresis of the colony PCR products revealed a band at approximately 5,683 bp, consistent with the theoretical value (Figure 4.1.2).

4.3 Ligation Reaction

Ligation reaction

Experiment

To verify whether the purified SUMO-

DogTag-TVN fusion protein retained

DogTag-mediated conjugation activity, we used GFP-SnoopTag2 as a visual reporter protein and SnoopLigase2 to catalyze covalent ligation between

DogTag and SnoopTag2. The reaction systems contained either SUMO-

DogTag-TVN or SUMO-DogTag lacking

TVNFKLY. A negative control lacking

SnoopLigase2 was also included to exclude higher-molecular-weight bands caused by protein mixing or nonspecific aggregation. Each group was reacted at room temperature for 15 min or 6 h.

After the reaction, SDS-PAGE loading buffer was added to terminate the reaction, and SDS-PAGE was used to compare the migration patterns of the substrate bands and the ligation- product bands.

Results

In the control group without

SnoopLigase2, GFP-SnoopTag2 and

SUMO-DogTag-TVN primarily retained their respective substrate bands, and no obvious higher-molecular-weight ligation product was observed. After

SnoopLigase2 was added, a new

higher-molecular-weight band

appeared above the substrate bands.

Its migration position was consistent with the expected molecular weight of the ligation product formed by GFP-

SnoopTag2 and the DogTag-containing protein.

SUMO-DogTag-TVN and SUMO-DogTag both showed the same type of enzyme- dependent band change, indicating that introduction of the TVNFKLY peptide did not substantially disrupt the ligation function of DogTag. A ligation product could already be observed after 15 min, and the corresponding band remained detectable after extending the reaction to 6 h.

Therefore, these results support the conclusion that the purified SUMO-

DogTag-TVN retained detectable

SnoopLigase2-dependent conjugation activity.

4.4 Functional Validation

4.4.1 FITC Fluorescence Labeling

FITC fluorescence labeling

Experiment

To track the distribution of the fusion protein during magnetic-nanoparticle incubation, magnetic separation, and washing, we fluorescently labeled the purified protein with fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC).

The protein was placed in a carbonate buffer suitable for the reaction between

FITC and protein amino groups. FITC was slowly added under light-protected conditions, and the labeling reaction was allowed to proceed. After the reaction, glycine was added to terminate the remaining FITC-labeling reaction, and unreacted free dye was removed using a desalting column [6].

The control protein was subjected to the same labeling and post-treatment procedures.

Small amounts of FITC-labeled protein and unlabeled protein were analyzed by SDS-PAGE. The nonfluorescent half of the gel was immersed in Coomassie

Brilliant Blue G250 rapid staining solution, while the side containing the

FITC-labeled protein was kept protected from light and was not stained. Images were acquired using the 532 nm and 302 nm imaging channels. One portion was used to observe protein migration and loading, and the other was used to compare the fluorescence signals of the labeled and unlabeled samples.

Results

Gel imaging showed a clear fluorescence signal in the FITC-labeled protein lane, whereas the unlabeled protein lane displayed only weak background. The fluorescence signal largely corresponded to the protein- band region, supporting the conclusion that FITC was associated with the protein sample rather than that the signal was produced entirely by free dye in the gel.

These results indicate that the labeled fusion protein had a fluorescence signal suitable for subsequent microscopic

observation. However, because the dye-

to-protein molar ratio was not

measured and standardized exposure

and band-density analysis were not

performed, the present results only

confirm successful labeling and cannot

be used to calculate FITC labeling

efficiency or directly compare labeling

levels among different protein samples.

4.4.2 Magnetic-Nanoparticle Binding and Washing

Magnetic-nanoparticle binding and washing

Experiment

To preliminarily evaluate the binding of

SUMO-DogTag-TVN to magnetic nanoparticles and its retention after washing, the FITC-labeled fusion protein was co-incubated with Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles. The experimental group used the fusion protein containing TVNFKLY, whereas the control group used the control protein containing GTWSLLL. Protein input, particle amount, incubation time, and buffer system were kept as consistent as possible.

A magnetic separator was used to collect the magnetic nanoparticles and remove the original dispersion medium. The labeled-protein reaction mixture was then added and thoroughly resuspended. Co- incubation was performed at room temperature in the dark, with periodic gentle mixing to ensure sufficient contact between the protein and the particles.

After incubation, the magnetic nanoparticles were collected using the magnetic rack and the supernatant was removed. The particles were then washed multiple times with buffer to reduce the retention of unbound protein and free fluorescent material.

After washing, the particles were gently resuspended, and bright-field and green-fluorescence images were acquired to determine whether the fluorescence signal remained associated with the particle fraction.

Results

After magnetic separation and multiple washes, green fluorescence could still be observed in particles or particle- aggregation regions in some microscopic fields, indicating that FITC- labeled material could be retained with the magnetic-particle fraction in this experimental workflow. Under the

action of the magnetic field, the

magnetic nanoparticles changed

from a disordered state to an ordered

arrangement, and the green

fluorescence aligned accordingly. This result provided qualitative evidence for magnetic-field-guided changes in SELP orientation [7].

5 GAG Retention Module

GAG Retention Module

Plasmid Construction and Recombinant Protein Production

Experiment

The GAG-retention module required a recombinant protein that could be stably expressed while remaining compatible with downstream functional validation. Therefore, we adopted a modular fusion protein design: the His tag was used for protein purification, SUMO was used to facilitate recombinant protein expression and processing, the AviTag was used for subsequent BirA-mediated enzymatic biotinylation, the DogTag-containing region was used for modular conjugation, and the CPC sequence served as the core GAG-interacting domain.

After plasmid construction, the recombinant expression plasmid was confirmed and the correct construct was introduced into *E. coli* BL21(DE3). Expression samples were then analyzed to evaluate the production of the target fusion protein and its solubility distribution, and the established expression conditions were used for subsequent large-scale protein preparation.

The obtained His-SUMO-AviTag-TEVsite-linker-DogTag-CPC fusion protein was further purified by His-tag affinity chromatography. By comparing the distribution of the target protein among different purification fractions, we confirmed the recovery of the recombinant protein and obtained the target protein fractions for subsequent processing. This established the upstream experimental workflow from plasmid construction → recombinant protein production → purified fusion protein.

Results

1.1 Design of Expression Plasmids

Using the pET-28a(+) backbone, we designed three expression plasmids: pET-28a(+)-CPC, pET-28a(+)-LinkN, and pET-28a(+)-CPC+LinkN, with full lengths of 5,827 bp, 5,805 bp, and 5,887 bp, respectively (Table 1.1.1 and Figure 1.1.1). All three constructs used the same expression framework, containing a T7 promoter, lac operator, and kanamycin (Kan) resistance gene. From the N-terminus to the C-terminus, each target fusion protein contained a 6×His tag, SUMO fusion tag, TEV cleavage site, linker, CPC and/or Link-N sequence, AviTag, and DogTag. In the CPC+LinkN construct, CPC and Link-N were connected by a linker.

The three constructs differed only in their inserted sequences (Table 1.1.1): the CPC construct contained the CPC sequence; the Link-N construct contained Link-N and served as a CPC-free control; and the CPC+LinkN construct contained both CPC and Link-N, allowing us to assess whether Link-N fusion affected CPC-mediated GAG interactions.

1.2 Expression of CPC Recombinant Proteins and Optimization of Induction Conditions

The synthesized plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) for protein expression. Colonies were obtained on Kan-containing plates for the transformed constructs (Figure 1.2.1), whereas no colonies grew on the control (CK) plate without plasmid transformation.

Figure 1.2.1. Colonies after transformation of E. coli BL21(DE3) with pET-28a(+)-CPC, pET-28a(+)-LinkN, and pET-28a(+)-CPC+LinkN. All plates contained Kan. Upper left: negative control without plasmid transformation (CK); upper right: CPC; lower left: LinkN; lower right: CPC+LinkN.

We then performed small-scale induction screening of the CPC expression system in E. coli BL21(DE3). The initial construct contained a repetitive CPC sequence designed in-house. We compared different IPTG concentrations, induction temperatures, and induction durations. After colony PCR validation, transformants were induced with 0.1–1.0 mM IPTG at 16 °C for 16 h or at 30 °C for 6 h. Additional conditions included 37 °C for 4 h and induction at 30 °C for 9 h or 16 h. Repeated SDS-PAGE analyses of the supernatant and pellet fractions revealed no clear induced bands at the expected positions; target bands were weak or diffuse, and background bands were also present in some uninduced samples. Consistent with these observations, His-tag affinity purification of both small- and large-scale cultures failed to enrich a clearly identifiable target protein: proteins were visible in the lysate and flow-through, but the eluate contained no band or only a very weak one (see Notebook). Thus, expanding the range of induction conditions alone did not resolve the expression bottleneck.

We therefore redesigned the CPC coding sequence using the literature-reported CPC+14A sequence, RRRR(AARRR)₃R, and performed codon optimization for E. coli while reducing sequence repetitiveness at the DNA level. The redesigned expression system yielded detectable CPC-containing recombinant proteins: SDS-PAGE showed identifiable target bands (Figure 1.2.2A), although some basal expression remained. The final induction condition was 30 °C with 0.5 mM IPTG for 16 h. SDS-PAGE after affinity purification showed enrichment of the target protein in the eluate (Figure 1.2.2B). Western blotting detected Link-N, CPC, and CPC–Link-N at the expected molecular-weight positions (Figure 1.2.2C), confirming successful expression of the target proteins. A weaker band was also visible in the uninduced control, indicating a degree of leaky expression.

Protein Concentration and SUMO Removal

Experiment

After affinity purification, the recombinant protein was subjected to centrifugal ultrafiltration. This step was used to increase the protein concentration while simultaneously performing buffer exchange, thereby transferring the protein into conditions suitable for subsequent enzymatic cleavage.

The fusion protein was then treated with ULP1 to remove the SUMO domain. This step was performed because the downstream functional experiments focused on the actual CPC-containing functional construct rather than the complete expression fusion protein. At the same time, the AviTag was retained, allowing the processed protein to undergo BirA-mediated biotinylation and subsequent immobilization on streptavidin magnetic beads.

After SUMO cleavage, the sample was further analyzed to confirm tag removal and was subjected to another round of ultrafiltration to complete protein concentration and buffer exchange.After ULP1 cleavage, the final functional protein is AviTag-TEVsite-linker-DogTag-CPC.

Results

BCA quantification yielded concentrations of 0.30 mg/mL for Link-N, 0.21 mg/mL for CPC, and 0.19 mg/mL for CPC–Link-N (Figures 1.4.1b–d).

**Conjugation Activity Validation**

Experiment

Because the target CPC peptide is relatively small and therefore difficult to detect directly by electrophoresis, we introduced a GFP-SnoopTag reporter protein to examine whether the recovered CPC peptide retained DogTag-mediated conjugation activity. The CPC peptide and control peptide were subjected to conjugation reactions in parallel, with corresponding reactions lacking SnoopLigase included as controls.

After addition of the ligase, higher-molecular-weight bands corresponding to the conjugation products were observed, supporting the retention of DogTag-mediated conjugation activity by the CPC peptide. This model reaction also provided a readily detectable basis for validating the site-specific conjugation of CPC to the SELP scaffold in subsequent experiments. The assay validates the protein conjugation step and does not directly demonstrate successful anchoring of CPC within the SELP hydrogel.

Results

2.1 Validation of DogTag-Mediated Ligation Activity

Because the short peptides themselves have low molecular weights, their ligation After SnoopLigase2 was added, higher-molecular-weight bands consistent with SnoopTag2-GFP ligation products were observed at 55–70 kDa in lanes 1, 3, and 5 (red box in Figure 2.1.1). These bands disappeared or were markedly weaker in the corresponding ligase-free controls (lanes 2, 4, and 6). A ligation-product band was also observed at approximately 55 kDa in lane 7 (SUMO–DogTag control). These results support the conclusion that the recovered constructs retained DogTag-mediated ligation activity and could undergo specific ligation with SnoopTag2-GFP.

CS-A Electrophoretic Mobility Analysis

Experiment

We first examined whether the recombinant protein could interact with CS-A. CS-A is an important sulfated GAG in the cartilage extracellular matrix, while CPC is enriched in positively charged amino acids. We therefore expected that interaction between CPC and negatively charged CS-A would alter the migration behavior of CS-A in the electrophoresis system.

Before conducting the protein–GAG experiments, CS-A was first analyzed independently to confirm that a detectable GAG signal could be obtained under the established electrophoresis and staining conditions. The migration of CS-A was then compared under different protein conditions, with particular attention to whether increasing protein levels caused reduced migration distance, broader bands, or increased retention near the loading wells. This provided a direct molecular-level evaluation of the interaction between the recombinant protein and sulfated GAGs.

This experiment was primarily used as a binding screen. Because CS-A is a heterogeneous and polydisperse polymer, changes in electrophoretic mobility are suitable for determining whether an interaction occurs and assessing its relative changes.

This experiment therefore primarily addressed the first key question of the GAG-retention module:

Can the engineered CPC-containing recombinant protein still directly interact with sulfated GAGs at the molecular level?

Results

2.2 Establishment and Optimization of the CS-A Agarose Electrophoretic Mobility Assay

To directly assess interactions between CPC-containing recombinant proteins and sulfated GAGs, we first established a CS-A agarose electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA). CS-A alone and CS-A mixed with 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, or 10 µM SUMO–CPC, SUMO–CPC–Link-N, or SUMO–Link-N were analyzed by agarose gel electrophoresis (16 lanes in total), followed by toluidine blue staining. The initial electrophoresis duration was approximately 50 min, with bromophenol blue as the tracking dye. CS-A migrated substantially faster than bromophenol blue and had migrated too far by the end of the 50-min run for reliable comparison. Although CS-A was clearly visible, none of the proteins—including the CPC-free SUMO–Link-N control—caused an obvious change in migration distance, band width, or retention near the loading wells (see Notebook). These results indicated that the initial electrophoresis duration was unsuitable for the current CS-A detection system.

To rule out problems with the detection system itself, we analyzed CS-A alone at different loading amounts (1, 2, 5, and 10 µg). The CS-A-only controls produced clear, detectable GAG bands, and band intensity increased with loading amount (Figure 2.2.1), demonstrating that the current agarose electrophoresis and toluidine blue staining system could detect CS-A. The electrophoresis duration was therefore shortened to approximately 30–40 min.

Figure 2.2.1. Establishment and optimization of the CS-A agarose electrophoretic mobility assay. Different amounts of CS-A (1, 2, 5, and 10 µg) were electrophoresed individually on an agarose gel and stained with toluidine blue.

After the electrophoresis duration was optimized, CS-A consistently appeared in a more suitable region of the gel for analysis. However, when different concentrations of CPC-containing fusion proteins were mixed with CS-A and analyzed again, no clear concentration-dependent mobility shift was observed. In other words, the system reliably detected CS-A, but adding the proteins did not produce a sufficiently clear migration change. Thus, the CS-A detection system was successfully established and optimized, but no clear positive CPC–CS-A readout was obtained through a mobility shift. This result does not directly demonstrate that CPC lacks GAG-binding activity, because migration may also be affected by molecular size, charge, conformation, and the state of the protein samples.

AviTag-Mediated GAG Capture Assay

Experiment

To complement the electrophoretic mobility assay, we established a second functional validation approach based on protein immobilization and GAG quantification.

Following ULP1 treatment, the recombinant protein retained the AviTag and was therefore first subjected to site-specific biotinylation using BirA. After biotinylation, free biotin was removed by desalting, and the protein concentration was re-measured by BCA. Biotinylation efficiency was verified by streptavidin gel shift or streptavidin-HRP Western blotting.The protein was then immobilized on streptavidin magnetic beads through the biotin–streptavidin interaction, thereby establishing an immobilized protein–GAG interaction system.

The immobilized protein was subsequently incubated with CS-A. After magnetic separation, the supernatant was collected and the remaining soluble CS-A was quantified using the DMMB assay.

Unlike the electrophoretic mobility assay, this experiment focused on whether immobilized protein could reduce the amount of CS-A remaining in solution. Naked magnetic bead controls and input controls were included to distinguish protein-dependent GAG capture from nonspecific adsorption by the magnetic beads and to determine the total amount of GAG at the beginning of the reaction.

Therefore, the primary readout of this experiment was the relative capture efficiency of CS-A by the immobilized protein.

From Molecular Binding to the GAG-Retention Design

The two experimental approaches validated the same molecular basis from different perspectives.

The CS-A electrophoretic mobility assay examined whether the CPC-containing protein altered the migration behavior of CS-A, whereas the streptavidin magnetic bead–DMMB assay further examined whether the immobilized protein could capture CS-A from solution.

Together, the two assays established a stepwise validation chain:

Plasmid construction → recombinant CPC protein production → purification and SUMO removal → protein–GAG interaction → GAG capture.

Results

2.3 CS-A Capture Assay Using an AviTag-Based Immobilization System

2.3.1 Site-Specific Biotinylation of AviTag

Biotinylation was assessed by SDS-PAGE, using non-biotinylated protein as the control (Figure 2.3.1.1). After incubation of non-biotinylated Link-N with SA, a free Link-N band was visible at approximately 15 kDa (red arrow). In contrast, this band disappeared or was markedly weaker when biotinylated Link-N, CPC, or CPC–Link-N was incubated with SA, while higher-molecular-weight bands associated with SA-containing complexes appeared near 70 kDa (red box). These observations suggest successful biotinylation and indicate that the resulting proteins could bind to streptavidin magnetic beads, establishing a basis for the subsequent protein–GAG interaction assay.

LinkN, CPC, and CPC–LinkN recombinant proteins containing AviTag were site-specifically biotinylated using BirA ligase. The biotinylated proteins and a non-biotinylated control were then incubated with free streptavidin (SA) for 30 min. Molecular-weight markers on the left are labeled from 15 to 70 kDa. From left to right, the lanes contain: non-biotinylated LinkN + SA (control), biotinylated LinkN + SA, biotinylated CPC + SA, and biotinylated CPC–LinkN + SA. 2.3.3 Statistical Analysis of the Reduction in Supernatant CS-A Associated with CPC and CPC–Link-N

To avoid drawing mechanistic conclusions directly from visual observations, we specified statistical hypotheses and applied multiple-comparison correction. This analysis assessed whether the reduction in supernatant CS-A was supported by statistical evidence and defined the scope of the conclusions that could be drawn.

CPC was compared with CK, and CPC–Link-N was compared with CK. Because each of the three treatment measurements corresponded one-to-one with a CK measurement, paired t-tests were used. For CPC versus CK, the difference for the $`i`$th pair was defined as:

``` math d_{i} = C_{CPC,i} - C_{CK,i} ```

If CPC captures more CS-A, the amount of residual CS-A in the supernatant after treatment should decrease; that is, we expect $`d_{i} < 0`$. Accordingly, the hypotheses for the prespecified one-sided test were: $`H_{0}:\mu_{d} = 0`$; $`H_{1}:\mu_{d} < 0`$. Here, $`\mu_{d}`$ denotes the population mean difference between the treatment group and the CK control. The same hypotheses were used to compare CPC–Link-N with CK.

The paired t-statistic is defined as: $`t = \frac{\overline{d}}{\frac{s_{d}}{\sqrt{n}}}`$, where $`\overline{d}`$ and $`s_{d}`$ denote the mean and standard deviation of the paired differences, respectively. The number of pairs was $`n = 3`$, giving $`df = n - 1 = 2`$; the one-sided p-value was calculated as $`p = P\left( T_{df} \leq t \right)`$.

The mean paired differences for CPC versus CK and CPC–Link-N versus CK were −39.73 µg/mL and −26.49 µg/mL, respectively. The raw p-values from the one-sided paired t-tests were 0.0314 and 0.0053, respectively (Figure 2.3.3.1). When the two prespecified comparisons were tested together, the Holm method was used to correct for multiple comparisons. The raw p-values, ranked from smallest to largest, were $`p_{(1)} = 0.0053,\ \ p_{(2)} = 0.0314`$, with the number of comparisons $`m = 2`$. The adjusted p-values were calculated as:

``` math p_{(1)}' = (m - 1 + 1) \times 0.0053 = 0.0106 ```

``` math p_{(2)}' = max\left( p_{(1)}',\ \ (m - 2 + 1) \times 0.0314 \right) = 0.0314 ```

After adjustment, the p-value for CPC–Link-N versus CK was 0.0106, and that for CPC versus CK was 0.0314. At a significance level of α = 0.05, both adjusted p-values were below 0.05; therefore, the null hypotheses that the mean differences between each treatment and CK were zero could be rejected.

In summary, the amount of residual CS-A in the supernatant was lower after treatment with both CPC and CPC–Link-N than in CK. Under the current dataset and analysis method, the results support an association between immobilized CPC or CPC–Link-N and reduced supernatant CS-A, in a direction consistent with the expected CPC-mediated GAG capture. However, because all measurements came from a single experiment (n = 3), this analysis should be considered exploratory.

Overview

To validate the molecular basis of our GAG-retention module, we established a complete experimental workflow spanning plasmid construction, recombinant protein preparation, tag removal, and functional validation. The overall strategy was to first obtain a purified recombinant protein that could be used in subsequent experiments while retaining the CPC functional module, and then directly evaluate whether the protein could interact with glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), particularly chondroitin sulfate A (CS-A).

Therefore, we constructed the His-SUMO-AviTag-TEVsite-linker-DogTag-CPC expression system and used *Escherichia coli* for recombinant protein production. Following expression and purification of the fusion protein by His-tag affinity chromatography, ultrafiltration was used to concentrate the protein and exchange the buffer. The SUMO domain was subsequently removed from the fusion protein using ULP1, followed by reverse purification using the His tag and another round of ultrafiltration to obtain a CPC-containing protein preparation suitable for subsequent functional validation.

The processed protein was then evaluated for GAG interaction from two complementary perspectives. First, changes in CS-A electrophoretic mobility were analyzed to qualitatively or semi-quantitatively evaluate protein–GAG interaction. Subsequently, the retained AviTag was used for BirA-mediated enzymatic biotinylation, allowing the protein to be immobilized on streptavidin magnetic beads, followed by DMMB-based analysis of its ability to capture soluble CS-A. In this way, we could first validate the molecular function of the protein-level functional module before introducing it into the final SELP hydrogel.

1\. Preparation of CPC Recombinant Proteins

To support subsequent validation of ligation activity and glycosaminoglycan (GAG) capture, we first prepared recombinant proteins containing the cationic peptide carrier (CPC). This section describes the design of the expression plasmids, establishment and optimization of the CPC recombinant-protein expression system, His-tag affinity purification and concentration, and SUMO-tag removal followed by reverse purification.

2. Validation of Ligation Activity and GAG-Binding Capability

After obtaining purified proteins, we first validated DogTag-mediated ligation activity. We then evaluated interactions between CPC-containing recombinant proteins and sulfated GAGs using a chondroitin sulfate A (CS-A) agarose electrophoretic mobility assay and an AviTag-based bead-immobilization assay with DMMB detection

Relationship to the Final SELP System

The experiments described above represent the molecular validation of the GAG-retention module. Their purpose was to determine whether the engineered CPC-containing protein retained the GAG interaction expected from the design.

Therefore, the current protein-level experiments first validate the molecular basis of CPC–GAG interaction, whereas whether CPC immobilized within the SELP hydrogel can truly reduce GAG loss represents a further material-level validation that requires direct evaluation through GAG retention/loss experiments in the hydrogel.

Through this approach, we progressively advanced the experimental logic from the smallest functional unit to the final biomaterial system:

engineered plasmid → recombinant protein → protein processing → molecular GAG interaction → GAG capture → hydrogel-level GAG retention.

GAG 保留模块

实验概述

为了验证 GAG 保留模块的分子基础，我们建立了一条从质粒构建、重组蛋白制备、标签去除到功能验证的完整实验链条。整个实验的思路是首先获得能够用于后续实验、且保留 CPC 功能模块的纯化重组蛋白，随后直接评价该蛋白是否能够与 glycosaminoglycans（GAG，糖胺聚糖），尤其是 chondroitin sulfate A（CS-A，硫酸软骨素 A）发生相互作用。

因此，我们构建了 His-SUMO-AviTag-TEVsite-linker-DogTag-CPC 表达体系，并利用 *Escherichia coli* 进行重组蛋白制备。表达并通过 His-tag affinity chromatography（His 标签亲和层析）纯化融合蛋白后，采用超滤对蛋白进行浓缩和缓冲液置换。随后使用 ULP1 对融合蛋白中的 SUMO 进行切除，利用his标签反向纯化，并再次通过超滤获得适用于后续功能验证的 CPC-containing protein preparation（含 CPC 蛋白样品）。

获得处理后的蛋白后，我们从两个互补角度评价其 GAG 相互作用。首先，通过观察 CS-A electrophoretic mobility（电泳迁移率）的变化，对蛋白–GAG 相互作用进行定性或半定量分析；随后利用保留下来的 AviTag 进行 BirA 酶促生物素化，将蛋白固定到 streptavidin magnetic beads（链霉亲和素磁珠）上，并结合 DMMB 方法检测其对可溶性 CS-A 的捕获能力。这样，我们可以在将功能模块引入最终 SELP 水凝胶之前，首先验证其蛋白水平的分子功能。

质粒构建与重组蛋白制备

GAG 保留模块需要一种既能够稳定表达，又能够兼容后续功能验证的重组蛋白。因此，我们采用模块化融合蛋白设计：His tag 用于蛋白纯化，SUMO 用于辅助重组蛋白的表达和处理，AviTag 用于后续 BirA 酶促生物素化，DogTag-containing region 用于模块化连接，而 CPC 序列则作为核心的 GAG-interacting domain（GAG 相互作用结构域）。

完成质粒构建后，对重组表达质粒进行确认，并将正确的表达构建体导入 *E. coli* BL21(DE3)。随后通过表达样品分析评价目标融合蛋白的获得情况及其可溶性分布，并将确定的表达条件用于后续较大规模的蛋白制备。

获得的 His-SUMO-AviTag-TEVsite-linker-DogTag-CPC 融合蛋白进一步通过 His-tag affinity chromatography 进行纯化。通过比较纯化过程中不同组分中的目标蛋白分布，确认重组蛋白的回收情况，并获得用于后续处理的目标蛋白组分。这一步建立了从 plasmid construction → recombinant protein production → purified fusion protein 的上游实验链条。

蛋白浓缩与 SUMO 去除

完成亲和层析后，对重组蛋白进行 centrifugal ultrafiltration（离心超滤）。这一过程用于提高蛋白浓度，同时进行 buffer exchange（缓冲液置换），从而将蛋白转移至适合后续酶切处理的条件。

随后使用 ULP1 对融合蛋白中的 SUMO 结构域进行去除。之所以进行这一步处理，是因为后续功能实验关注的是实际的 CPC-containing functional construct，而不是完整的表达融合蛋白。同时，AviTag 被保留下来，因此处理后的蛋白仍然能够通过 BirA 进行生物素化，并进一步固定到链霉亲和素磁珠上。

SUMO cleavage（SUMO 酶切）完成后，对样品进行进一步分析以确认标签去除情况，并再次进行 ultrafiltration（超滤），完成蛋白浓缩及缓冲液置换。ULP1 酶切后，最终获得的功能蛋白为 AviTag-TEVsite-linker-DogTag-CPC。

功能验证

连接活性验证

由于目标 CPC 短肽分子量较小，直接电泳检测存在困难，我们进一步引入 GFP-SnoopTag 报告蛋白，检验回收的 CPC 短肽是否保留 DogTag 介导的连接能力。CPC 短肽与对照肽分别进行连接反应，并设置不加入 SnoopLigase 的平行对照。

加入连接酶后出现了与连接产物相符的较高分子量条带，支持 CPC 短肽保留 DogTag 连接活性。该模型反应同时为后续 CPC 与 SELP 骨架的定点偶联提供了便于检测的连接验证基础。其验证范围为蛋白连接环节，不直接等同于完成了 CPC 在 SELP 水凝胶上的锚定。

CS-A 电泳迁移率分析

我们首先检测重组蛋白是否能够与 CS-A 发生相互作用。CS-A 是软骨 extracellular matrix（细胞外基质）中重要的 sulfated GAG，而 CPC 富含带正电的氨基酸，因此我们预期 CPC 与带负电的 CS-A 发生相互作用后，会改变 CS-A 在电泳体系中的迁移行为。

正式进行蛋白–GAG 实验之前，首先单独检测 CS-A，以确认在所建立的 electrophoresis 和 staining 条件下可以稳定观察到 GAG 信号。随后比较不同蛋白条件下 CS-A 的迁移情况，并观察随着蛋白水平增加，CS-A 是否出现迁移距离缩短、条带变宽或向加样孔附近滞留等变化。由此从分子水平直接评价重组蛋白与 sulfated GAG 的相互作用。

该实验主要作为 binding screen（结合筛选）。由于 CS-A 属于 heterogeneous and polydisperse polymer（异质、多分散高分子），电泳迁移率的改变适合用于判断相互作用是否发生及其相对变化。

该实验主要回答的是 GAG 保留模块的第一个核心问题：

工程化的 CPC-containing recombinant protein 是否仍然能够直接与 sulfated GAG 发生分子水平的相互作用？

AviTag 介导的 GAG 捕获实验

为了补充电泳迁移率实验，我们进一步建立了基于蛋白固定和 GAG 定量的第二条功能验证路线。

经过 ULP1 处理后，重组蛋白仍然保留 AviTag，因此首先利用 BirA 对其进行 site-specific biotinylation（位点特异性生物素化）。生物素化后经脱盐去除游离生物素，并以 BCA 重新定量；生物素化效率通过链霉亲和素凝胶迁移或链霉亲和素-HRP Western blot 验证。随后通过 biotin–streptavidin interaction（生物素–链霉亲和素相互作用）将蛋白固定到 streptavidin magnetic beads 上，从而建立一个固定化的 protein–GAG interaction system（蛋白–GAG 相互作用体系）。

随后将固定化蛋白与 CS-A 进行孵育，通过磁分离获得上清，并使用 DMMB assay 对剩余可溶性 CS-A 进行定量。

与前面的电泳迁移实验不同，这一实验关注的是“固定化蛋白是否能够使溶液中的 CS-A 减少”。实验同时设置 naked magnetic bead control（裸磁珠对照）和 input control（输入对照），从而区分 protein-dependent GAG capture（蛋白依赖性的 GAG 捕获）与磁珠本身的非特异性吸附，并确定反应开始时的 GAG 总量。。

因此，该实验的主要 readout（读出指标）是 immobilized protein 对 CS-A 的相对 capture efficiency（捕获效率）。

从分子结合到 GAG 保留设计

两条实验路线分别从不同角度验证相同的分子基础。

CS-A electrophoretic mobility assay 观察的是 CPC-containing protein 是否改变 CS-A 的迁移行为；而 streptavidin magnetic bead–DMMB assay 进一步检测 固定化蛋白是否能够从溶液中捕获 CS-A。

因此，两种实验共同建立了一条逐级推进的验证链：

质粒构建 → CPC 重组蛋白获得 → 纯化与 SUMO 去除 → 蛋白–GAG 相互作用 → GAG 捕获。

与最终 SELP 体系的关系

上述实验属于 GAG-retention module 的 molecular validation（分子层面验证）。其目的在于确认工程化 CPC-containing protein 是否保留设计所预期的 GAG interaction。

因此，目前的蛋白实验首先验证的是 CPC 与 GAG 相互作用这一分子基础；而 CPC 固定于 SELP 水凝胶后是否真正降低 GAG 流失，则属于进一步的 material-level validation（材料层面验证），需要通过水凝胶中的 GAG retention/loss 实验进行直接评价。

由此，我们将整个实验逻辑从最小功能单元逐步推进到最终 biomaterial system：

engineered plasmid → recombinant protein → protein processing → molecular GAG interaction → GAG capture → hydrogel-level GAG retention.
delivery:
As part of developing a modular carrier and delivery platform, we used mitochondria as a representative therapeutic cargo, prepared an engineered responsive peptide, evaluated its protein ligation activity and MMP-13 responsiveness, and characterized liposome–mitochondria complexes and their cellular delivery potential. With mitochondrial delivery as the initial

application, this module provides a foundation for a broader delivery platform that could be extended to other therapeutic cargoes through further optimization of the carrier formulation and cargo-specific validation.

6.1 Responsive Protein Expression and Functional Peptide Preparation

6.1.1 Expression Plasmid and Control Design

Expression plasmid and control design

Experiment

We designed the responsive construct pET28a-

MMP13sp and the scrambled control construct pET28a-Control using the pET-28a backbone. The responsive segment,

RRGPLGLSLGKR, was replaced with

RKGLSLGLPGRR in the control construct, preserving peptide length and amino acid composition while changing residue order. All other construct sequences were kept identical.

Both designs incorporated a 6×His tag, a

SUMO tag, a TEV protease cleavage site, a Cys conjugation site, and DogTag. GGGGS linkers were placed on either side of the responsive or control segment.

Results

The two plasmid designs were each 5691 bp long and shared a T7 promoter and a kanamycin resistance gene (Figures 1.1.1 and

1.1.2). Both encoded the same N-to-C- terminal arrangement: 6×His–SUMO–TEV cleavage site–Cys–GGGGS–responsive or control segment–GGGGS–DogTag. The responsive and control segments each contained 12 amino acids and differed only in residue order.

6.1.2 Plasmid Transformation and Antibiotic Selection

Plasmid transformation and antibiotic selection

Experiment

The two plasmids were separately transformed into Escherichia coli BL21(DE3).

Transformed cells were plated onto LB agar containing kanamycin, with an uninoculated plate included as a negative control.

Following incubation, individual colonies

were picked and expanded for protein expression.

Results

Multiple discrete colonies were observed on the experimental plates, whereas no visible colonies were detected on the uninoculated negative-control plate (Figure 1.2.1).

6.1.3 Fusion Protein Expression and Purification

Fusion protein expression and purification

Experiment

We screened IPTG induction conditions by comparing target protein expression across

IPTG concentrations, including 0.25 and 0.5 mM, with uninduced cultures as controls.

Bacterial lysates were separated into soluble supernatant and pellet fractions and analyzed by SDS-PAGE and Western blotting.

Expression and electrophoresis conditions were adjusted during optimization.

Responsive and control fusion proteins were produced at a larger scale under the selected conditions and purified separately by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. Lysate, flow- through, wash, and elution fractions were analyzed by SDS-PAGE. Fractions containing the target proteins were pooled and dialyzed, and protein concentrations were measured.

Results

Preliminary screening showed relatively prominent target protein bands at 0.25 and

0.5 mM IPTG. In both groups induced with

0.25 mM IPTG, bands in the 15–25 kDa range were enriched in the elution fractions, consistent with the expected size range of the fusion proteins (Figure 1.3.1).

One preparation of the responsive fusion protein had a measured concentration of 0.43 mg/mL; the corresponding control preparation had a measured concentration of

0.52 mg/mL.

6.1.4 TEV Protease Cleavage and Functional Peptide Release

6.1.4.1 TEV Cleavage and Peptide Recovery

TEV protease cleavage and functional peptide release

Experiment

Purified responsive fusion protein was incubated with TEV protease at 30 °C.

Samples were collected after 1, 2, and 4 h, alongside a control without TEV protease, and analyzed by SDS-PAGE.

Following cleavage, subtractive nickel-affinity chromatography was used to separate the target peptide from His-tagged components.

Recovered peptide samples were concentrated by lyophilization for downstream assays.

Results

Bands attributed to the released His/SUMO tag were observed in TEV-treated samples at

1, 2, and 4 h, with apparent molecular weights

in the 15–25 kDa range and migration distinct

from that of the uncleaved fusion protein

(Figure 1.4.1). A band corresponding to the added TEV protease was observed at approximately 27 kDa.

6.1.4.2 Ligation Activity of the Functional Peptide

TEV protease cleavage and functional peptide release

Experiment

The published SnoopLigase system catalyzes covalent isopeptide-bond formation between

DogTag and SnoopTagJr. This work established a basis for using SDS-PAGE mobility shifts to assess peptide ligation activity [1].

The recovered DogTag-containing peptide was mixed with GFP-SnoopTag and

SnoopLigase and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. SnoopLigase-mediated ligation of SUMO-DogTag to GFP-SnoopTag served as a positive control, and a reaction without SnoopLigase served as a negative control. Reaction products were analyzed by

SDS-PAGE.

Results

An additional band above the main GFP-

SnoopTag band appeared in the peptide reaction containing SnoopLigase relative to the negative control (Figure 1.4.2). This

mobility shift was consistent with the

formation of a peptide–GFP-SnoopTag

conjugate. SnoopLigase migrated to the 10–15 kDa range.

6.2 Construction and Characterization of the Liposomal Delivery System

6.2.1 Mitochondrial Isolation and Fraction Characterization

Mitochondrial isolation and fraction characterization

Experiment

TOMM20 (Tom20) is a receptor of the mitochondrial outer-membrane protein import machinery [2], whereas cytochrome c oxidase subunit IV (COX IV) is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane [3]. Their complementary localizations provided the rationale for assessing mitochondrial components from both membrane compartments.

Mitochondria were isolated from cultured cells, with the starting cell number adjusted during preparation optimization. Whole-cell samples, cytosolic supernatants, and mitochondrial pellets were analyzed by

Western blotting for TOMM20 and COX IV to examine the presence and distribution of mitochondrial components across fractions.

The isolated mitochondrial fraction was used for subsequent complex assembly.

Marker detection was interpreted as evidence of mitochondrial components; organelle purity, membrane integrity, and respiratory function require distinct assessments [3].

Results

TOMM20 and COX IV were both detected in the isolated pellet fraction (Figure 2.1.1),

indicating the presence of mitochondrial

components in the preparation.

6.2.2 Preparation of Functionalized Liposomes

Preparation of functionalized liposomes

Experiment

DOTAP and DOPE were selected as cationic and fusogenic lipid components, respectively.

A previous study used DOTAP/DOPE coatings to improve mitochondrial transfer, providing a rationale for investigating this lipid combination in our carrier system [4]. DSPE-

PEG-Mal was included to provide maleimide groups for conjugation with Cys-containing peptides, based on established peptide–PEG– lipid coupling chemistry [5].

Functionalized liposomes were prepared using DOPE, DOTAP, and DSPE-PEG-Mal and subsequently co-incubated with isolated mitochondria for complex assembly.

Results

The prepared liposome suspension had a

milky-white appearance (Figure 2.2.1).

6.2.3 Characterization of the Complexes

6.2.3.1 Confocal Fluorescence Characterization

Characterization of the complexes

Experiment

Liposomes and mitochondria were labeled with DiD and MitoTracker Green, respectively.

Following co-incubation, samples were examined by confocal fluorescence microscopy. Red and green fluorescence channels were acquired alongside bright-field images to assess the spatial distribution of the two components.

Results

DiD-labeled liposomes exhibited red fluorescence, and MitoTracker Green-labeled mitochondria exhibited green fluorescence.

The signals overlapped at multiple locations, appearing as yellow–orange regions in the merged image (Figure 2.3.1).

These observations support a spatial association between liposomes and

mitochondria, providing preliminary imaging

evidence for the formation of liposome–

mitochondria complexes during co- incubation. Whether this association involves membrane fusion requires further verification.

6.2.3.2 Structural Characterization by Transmission Electron Microscopy

Characterization of the complexes

Experiment

Functionalized liposomes, isolated mitochondria, and samples obtained after liposome–mitochondria co-incubation were

examined by transmission electron microscopy. Morphology and membrane-like structures were compared across the three sample types.

Results

Vesicle-like structures with visible membrane outlines were observed in the liposome samples (Figure 2.3.2A). In the complex

samples, peripheral membrane-like structures surrounded internal components

(Figure 2.3.2C). This morphology was

consistent with liposomal enclosure of

mitochondrial material.

6.2.4 Evaluation of Linker Peptide Conjugation to Liposomes

Evaluation of linker peptide conjugation to liposomes

Experiment

The conjugation strategy was based on thiol– maleimide coupling between a peptide cysteine residue and a maleimide- functionalized PEG–lipid [5].

The Cys-containing linker peptide was co- incubated with maleimide-functionalized liposomes, with liposomes lacking added peptide included as controls. Following incubation, ultrafiltration was used to separate unbound peptide from carrier- associated material. Colorimetric protein assays were used to evaluate peptide recovery and association with the liposomes.

Results

Ultrafiltration produced variable sample recovery and liposome loss, while the liposome formulation interfered with colorimetric protein detection. These effects prevented reliable distinction between free and carrier-associated peptide. Covalent conjugation could not be distinguished from nonspecific adsorption or losses during sample processing, and conjugation efficiency could not be reliably determined.

6.3 Functional Assessment

6.3.1 SnoopLigase Mediated Ligation of Responsive and Control Proteins

SnoopLigase-mediated ligation

Experiment

Responsive MMP13-DogTag and scrambled

Control-DogTag protein preparations were separately mixed with GFP-SnoopTag. Parallel reactions with and without SnoopLigase were analyzed by SDS-PAGE to compare ligation product formation between the two groups.

Results

A higher-molecular-weight band near 55 kDa was observed in both responsive and control reactions containing SnoopLigase (Figure

3.1.1). No distinct band at the same position was observed in the corresponding reactions

without SnoopLigase. The enzyme-associated

mobility shifts were consistent with formation

of ligation products in both groups.

6.3.2 MMP Responsive Cleavage of Reporter Conjugates

MMP-responsive cleavage

Experiment

MMP-13 was selected as a disease-relevant enzyme because Mmp13-deficient mice show reduced osteoarthritic cartilage erosion [6].

This finding motivated evaluation of MMP-13 responsiveness in the linker design.

Responsive peptide (Pep) and scrambled control peptide (Control) were separately ligated to GFP-SnoopTag to generate reporter substrates. The conjugates were treated with

MMP-13 under matched treatment conditions.

Samples were collected at 0, 2, 4, 6, and 24 h and analyzed by SDS-PAGE to compare bands

corresponding to intact conjugates and lower- molecular-weight species.

Results

At 2 h, the Control group retained a slower- migrating band near 35 kDa, assigned to the intact GFP–peptide conjugate, whereas the corresponding higher-molecular-weight band in the Pep group was weaker or not clearly detectable (Figure 3.2.1).

The observed difference was consistent with

cleavage of the responsive conjugate, but the available comparisons did not establish whether it arose from MMP-13 activity or differences in the initial composition of the reporter substrates.

6.3.3 Cellular Localization of Delivered Mitochondrial Tracers

Cellular localization of delivered mitochondrial tracers

Experiment

Isolated mitochondria were labeled with

MitoTracker Green and co-incubated with liposomes. The resulting complexes were added to recipient cell cultures. Hoechst

33342 and cell membrane staining provided nuclear and cellular reference points for multichannel confocal imaging, alongside bright-field images. The distribution of mitochondria-associated green fluorescence was compared between complex-treated cells and control cells.

Results

Green fluorescence was observed within the cell outlines and in perinuclear regions of complex-treated cells (Figure 3.3.1A). No distinct corresponding green fluorescence was observed in the control group (Figure

3.3.1B). These images showed cell-associated

localization of the mitochondrial tracer; they did not establish the intracellular integrity or function of the delivered mitochondria.

6.3.4 In Vitro Cytocompatibility of the Functional Peptide

In vitro cytocompatibility

Experiment

Reduction of WST-8 produces a water-soluble formazan signal and has been established as a colorimetric indicator of cell viability [7].

The assay was used here as a preliminary measure of peptide cytocompatibility.

Cells were treated with 5 or 10 μM functional peptide for 24, 48, or 72 h. A CCK-8 assay was used to assess relative cell viability, with control, blank, and peptide-treated groups included in the experimental design (Figure

3.4.1A).

Results

At 24 h, relative cell viability was approximately 70% in the 5 μM group and

55% in the 10 μM group. At 48 h, the values were approximately 85%–90% in both groups and were approximately 85%–95% at 72 h

(Figure 3.4.1B). At both concentrations, the measured values were lower at 24 h than at the later time points.

The relatively high cell viability observed at 48 and 72 h provides preliminary evidence of limited cytotoxicity of the functional peptide at these later time points under the tested

conditions, supporting its potential

cytocompatibility. However, the reduced viability at 24 h indicates that early cellular responses require further evaluation before conclusions about overall cytocompatibility can be drawn.
